lessons.title: Common HRA Mistakes, Fake Rent Receipts and Tax Notices

body.text: Most HRA trouble does not come from clever planning gone wrong. It comes from small errors repeated every year, and from shortcuts copied from colleagues, at a time when the department can match your claim against your landlord's return in seconds.

children.text: You now know how HRA is calculated, who can claim it, what proof it needs and how to file it. This lesson is the safety check: the mistakes that cost people money, the ones that cost them their exemption, and the handful that turn a tax matter into a penalty case.

body.caption: Seven ways a calculation goes wrong

cells: Using gross salary or CTC as "salary"
Salary for HRA is only basic, eligible DA and turnover commission
Recalculate with basic alone if you have no DA or commission (Lesson 5)
Forgetting to subtract 10% of salary from rent
Limit 2 is rent minus 10% of salary, not rent
Always run all three limits, not just the ones you remember
Using the city where you work
The 50% or 40% limit follows the city of your rented home
Use your rent agreement address (Lesson 6)
Assuming a metro means 50% automatically
Only eight named cities qualify, and only from tax year 2026-27. Gurugram, Noida, Thane and Navi Mumbai are not on the list
Check the list, and check the year
Adding up the whole year when rent, salary or city changed
The exemption is worked out period by period
Split the year at every change (Lesson 8)
Claiming the full flat rent when sharing
You can claim only the rent you actually bear
Claim your share, backed by your own transfers (Lesson 11)
Counting deposits, brokerage, maintenance or electricity as rent
Only rent for the accommodation counts
Strip these out before you calculate

body.title: One mistake, one number: gross salary instead of basic

body.text: Notice which way this error cuts. Using the bigger salary figure raised the amount subtracted from rent, so the employee under-claimed by ₹90,000. Plenty of HRA mistakes cost you money rather than saving it, which is why a yearly recheck is worth the twenty minutes.

cells: Claiming HRA while in the new regime
The exemption is simply not available. Choose the old regime with your employer and in your return
Never declaring the old regime to your employer
Higher TDS all year, and a refund that arrives months later
Missing the employer proof deadline
A TDS catch-up in February and March, though the exemption survives in your return
Filing a belated return
Usually fatal for HRA: a salaried person cannot opt out of the new regime in a belated return
No landlord PAN when annual rent exceeds ₹1,00,000
The employer can refuse the exemption, and the claim looks incomplete in any enquiry
Paying rent in cash with no trail
Receipts alone rarely satisfy an officer who asks how the money moved
Not deducting TDS on rent above ₹50,000 a month
Interest and late fees for you, and a credit problem for your landlord (Lesson 16)
Claiming rent for a home you own or live in rent-free
The claim fails the basic tests and is treated as a false claim

children.text: The department does not need to visit your flat to test an HRA claim. It matches data it already holds.

cells: Your landlord's PAN in Form 124 and your return
Whether the rent you claim appears as income in your landlord's return
Form 141 for TDS on rent
Independent confirmation of rent paid, landlord and amount, above ₹50,000 a month
Your Form 130 against your return
A gap between what your employer allowed and what you claimed
AIS and Form 26AS
Your salary, TDS and other reported transactions in one place
The relationship field in Form 124
Rent paid to a parent, spouse or other relative, for closer checking
Repeated PANs across employees
The same landlord PAN used by many colleagues, a pattern that stands out immediately

events.title: A PAN raises a flag
events.description: News reports described rent of roughly ₹1 crore being attributed to one PAN. The person named said they had never received any such rent.

events.title: Data matching widens
events.description: Reports said 8,000 to 10,000 high-value cases, each above ₹10 lakh, were identified where rent claimed did not match rent reported by the recipient. Some employees at the same company had used identical landlord PANs.

events.title: CBDT responds
events.description: The Board called reports of a special drive to reopen cases baseless, and said verification covered a small number of high-value mismatches for financial year 2020-21, not a bulk reopening.

events.title: The checks are built into the form
events.description: Form 124 now captures the landlord relationship alongside PAN, so mismatches are visible at source rather than years later.

body.text: Your employer accepting your receipts is not protection. The employer only checks that the paperwork looks complete for TDS. Whether the rent was genuinely paid is between you and the tax department, and the question can be raised long after that employer has issued your Form 130.

children.text: Under Section 439 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 270A of the 1961 Act), the penalty is 50% of the tax on under-reported income, rising to 200% where income is misreported, which includes false claims and fabricated documents. Interest runs on top, and the tax itself is still payable.

stats.label: Penalty if treated as misreporting
stats.context: 200% of the tax, on top of the ₹93,600

children.text: So a ₹3,00,000 claim that cannot be supported can cost ₹2,80,800 before interest. If the same claim is treated as under-reporting rather than misreporting, the penalty is ₹46,800. The difference between the two usually comes down to whether the claim looks like an honest error or a fabricated one.

body.title: Try It: The Cost of a Bad Claim
body.prompt: Neeraj wrongly claims an HRA exemption of ₹2,00,000 while in the 30% slab. The claim is treated as misreporting. What is the penalty alone, at 200% of the tax on the misreported amount, including 4% cess in the tax? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: Tax on ₹2,00,000 at 30% plus 4% cess is ₹62,400. The penalty at 200% of that tax is ₹1,24,800, payable in addition to the ₹62,400 of tax and interest.

body.title: Quick Check: Error or Misreporting?
body.question: Which of these is most likely to be treated as misreporting rather than an honest error?
options: Using gross salary instead of basic salary in the three limits
Claiming rent for the full year when the tenant moved into an owned flat in January, by oversight
Submitting receipts and a PAN for a landlord who never received any rent
Using 50% instead of 40% for a flat in Noida
body.explanation: The first, second and fourth are calculation or record-keeping errors. Tax, interest and possibly a 50% penalty may follow, but they are arguable as honest mistakes. Submitting receipts for rent that was never paid, with someone else's PAN, is a false claim supported by false documents, which is what the 200% misreporting penalty is aimed at.

body.title: Scenario: The Notice Arrives
body.scenario: In November 2027, Ankit receives a communication about his return for tax year 2026-27. It says the HRA exemption of ₹3,60,000 he claimed does not match the rental income reported by the PAN he gave as his landlord. Ankit did pay rent: ₹30,000 a month by bank transfer to his landlord in Pune, with a registered agreement. He suspects his landlord simply did not report the rent.
body.prompt: How should Ankit respond, and what should he not do?
body.modelAnswer: He should respond on the e-filing portal within the time given, rather than ignoring it. His reply should attach the registered rent agreement, the monthly receipts, a bank statement highlighting twelve transfers to the landlord, and the calculation of the exemption showing salary for HRA, rent and the city percentage. He should tell his landlord about the mismatch, since the landlord may need to correct their own return, but he should not ask the landlord to create any backdated document. He should not withdraw a genuine claim out of fear, and he should not file a revised return removing the exemption unless he finds a real error in his own working. A documented, honest claim is usually accepted, and the landlord failing to declare the income is the landlord's problem, not evidence that Ankit did not pay.

body.title: Your Annual HRA Self-Audit
steps: Confirm the old regime is worth it for you this year, comparing both regimes before you claim
Recalculate the three limits using basic plus eligible DA, actual rent and the city of your home
Split the year at every change in rent, salary, HRA or city
Check that every rupee claimed left your bank account and reached the landlord
Confirm the landlord PAN you reported is valid and matches the landlord's name
Compare your figure with Form 130 and note the reason for any difference
File the original return by the due date, and keep your evidence file for years, not months

cards.definition: Income assessed higher than reported, attracting a penalty of 50% of the tax on the difference under Section 439 (Section 270A of the 1961 Act).
Deliberate false claims or fabricated documents, attracting a penalty of 200% of the tax on the misreported amount.
Comparing your HRA claim against your landlord's return through PAN, plus Form 130, AIS and TDS records.
Claiming less than you are entitled to, usually by using the wrong salary figure or forgetting a limit. It costs you money quietly.
A yearly recheck of regime choice, the three limits, period splits, money trail and landlord PAN before you file.

points: The most common calculation errors are using gross salary, ignoring the 10% subtraction, using your office city and pooling a year in which things changed
Some mistakes cost you money rather than saving it, so recheck your own claim even if nobody questions it
Compliance slips, especially filing a belated return, can cost you the exemption entirely
Claims are tested by matching your landlord's PAN against their return, plus Form 130, AIS and TDS records
A wrong claim costs tax plus interest plus a penalty of 50%, or 200% where it is treated as misreporting under Section 439
If a notice arrives for a genuine claim, answer it with the agreement, receipts, bank trail and your calculation, and do not withdraw a correct claim
